newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA says won't risk higher inflation for jobs.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA says won't risk higher inflation for jobs.

text.p: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Ian Macfarlane said on Thursday that Australia's unemployment rate was too high and in greater need of improvement than inflation, but slashing interest rates at the cost of higher inflation was not the way to correct the problem.

"Clearly, with the unemployment rate at 8.8 percent and the inflation rate at 2.4 percent, we would all have to agree that it is the former which is in the greater need of improvement," Macfarlane told a business dinner.
"Unfortunately, there is no panacea - the answer will not be found in any single breakthrough of policy," he said.
Every policy and every practice should be reviewed to see whether it was contributing to or inhibiting the growth of employment, and that included monetary policy, said Macfarlane.
Monetary policy was set in a way which let the economy grow as fast as possible without breaking the inflation objective of around 2.5 percent over the medium term, but no faster, he said.
Settings in recent years had been consistent with low inflation on average and a good rate of economic growth, he added.

"Even so, some might argue for an easier monetary policy - effectively saying 'why not ease monetary policy as much as is necessary to encourage faster growth, even if it pushes up inflation?'" he said.
"The problem with this approach is that it does not work," Macfarlane said.

Faster growth may be achieved for a short period and there may be a short-term fall in unemployment but in the medium term the result is higher inflation and higher unemployment, he said. "You cannot buy a better unemployment performance by accepting a worse inflation one," Macfarlane said.
"It therefore follows that the most useful thing monetary policy can do in the long run for employment is to encourage sustainable low inflation expansions," Macfarlane said.
But the RBA also had to make sure it did not become too risk-averse and impose too restrictive a speed limit on the economy, he said.

This would be the case if it had failed to take into account factors which were holding prices down -- such as the globalisation of the world economy and technological change and reductions in tariffs -- while at the same time opening up possibilities for faster growth.
"There certainly are many such factors," Macfarlane said.
"They are making the job of conducting monetary policy easier, but they are not causing us to over-achieve on inflation," he added.
